name: Toucouleur Empire
summary: A jihad state founded by El Hadj Umar Tall in 1852 across today’s Mali and Senegal; it conquered Ségou and Hamdullahi but was conquered by France in 1890–93.

location.value: West Africa. It began in Senegal and the Fouta Djallon (Guinea), took Nioro in 1855 as its capital and ruled from Segou after 1861. The page does not mention Timbuktu.

terrain.value: Savanna plains and low plateaus, the Niger’s inland delta floodplain around Ségou and Masina, and the Bandiagara cliffs.

climate.value: Sahel and Sudan savanna climate: a hot dry season and short summer rains, wetter in the south and drier toward the Sahara.

resources.value: Millet and rice farmland, cattle on the floodplains, gold from Bambuk and Buré, and control of river and caravan trade.

disasters.value: Droughts and poor harvests; wars and sieges in the 1850s–1860s caused famine in conquered regions.

population.value: The page gives no population figure.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Thousands of followers from Futa Toro moved east with Umar from the 1850s to settle and garrison the conquered lands.

economicBase.value: Taxes (religious and secular) and customs duties on trade; insecurity and the arms trade shifted trade from north–south Niger routes to an east–west axis linking Nioro and Segou. Millet, rice and cattle are not mentioned in the part of the page read.

tradeRoutes.value: River trade on the Niger and Senegal; caravans carried gold, grain and captives, and traders bought guns from French and British posts.

wealth.value: Wealth came from war booty, tribute and the treasuries of conquered capitals such as Ségou and Hamdullahi.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, market taxes and trade goods; cowrie shells in many markets.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: An Islamic state founded by Umar Tall, who returned from the Hajj as caliph of the Tijaniyya brotherhood of the Sudan; his son Ahmadu was enthroned as successor and Amir al-Mu’minin. Qadis and marabouts handled justice and Islamisation, and the state was funded by religious and secular taxes and customs duties.

keyRulers.value: Umar Tall (killed 1864) and his son Ahmadu, who continued to reign at Ségou and moved his court to Nioro after a revolt by his brother Muntaga in 1884.

succession.value: Ahmadu succeeded his father in 1864, but his brothers ruled their own provinces, such as Nioro, and challenged his authority.

institutions.value: Islamic courts using sharia, governors drawn from Umar’s family and disciples, and garrisons in fortified towns.

stability.value: Revolts by Bambara and Fula subjects were frequent; Masina rose against Umar in 1863–64, leading to his death.

eliteConflict.value: Umar’s sons quarrelled after his death; Ahmadu fought his brothers in the 1870s and 1880s to keep control.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry with muskets and later breech-loaders bought from Europeans, cavalry, and fortified stone forts (tata).

majorWars.value: Djenné fell quickly, followed by Hamdullahi in May 1862; rebels retook Hamdullahi in February 1864 and Umar Tall fled but was killed soon after.

territoryChange.value: Conquered Kaarta (1855), Ségou (1861) and Masina (1862) quickly, then lost all of them to France in 1890–93.

alliancesRivals.value: Fought the French in Senegal and the Fula state of Masina; signed treaties with France (1880s) before the final French conquest.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; its strength lay in Islamic scholarship and the organisation of armies.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to Muslim scholars and to trade for guns, but hostile to French expansion and to non-Muslim rulers.

communicationTransport.value: Footpaths, horses and messengers, and canoes on the Niger and Senegal rivers.

religion.value: Islam with the Tijaniyya order: Umar Tall returned from the Hajj as caliph of the Tijaniyya brotherhood of the Sudan.

languageWriting.value: Fula (Pulaar) was spoken by the Toucouleur elite; Arabic for religion and letters; Bambara among many subjects.

artsArchitecture.value: Mud-brick mosques and fortified palaces in towns such as Ségou, Nioro and Dinguiraye, plus Arabic manuscripts.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to Umar’s family, to the Tijaniyya order and to Islam, rather than to one people.

dailyLife.value: Most people lived in farming villages, growing millet and rice, herding cattle and paying tribute.

neighbours.value: French Senegal to the west, the Fula state of Masina, the Bambara kingdom of Ségou, and later Samori Ture’s empire to the south.

ideasReligions.value: Part of the West African jihad tradition that also created the Sokoto Caliphate; it spread the Tijaniyya order.

colonisation.value: French forces under Louis Archinard took Ségou (1890), Nioro (1891) and Bandiagara (1893).

riseSignals.value: After conquering Tamba (its king Yambi was beaten in September 1852) Umar Tall launched his jihad; he won the Battle of Ségou on 10 March 1861 and made the city his capital.

peakPeriod.value: Umar took Segou in March 1861 and Hamdullahi fell in May 1862; the page’s map shows the greatest extent at the time of Umar’s death in 1864.

declineSignals.value: Umar was killed near Bandiagara (1864) during the Masina revolt, and the state split among his heirs.

outcome.value: The French captured Nioro in 1891 and drove Ahmadu to Bandiagara; the text says the French took final control in 1893, ending the empire, while the infobox gives 1903.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Toucouleur Empire (checked 13 Nov 2026); Britannica: Tukulor empire (checked 15 Nov 2026) (Britannica says Ahmadu was defeated by the French in 1893 and the empire was absorbed into French territory, which supports 1893; it does not mention Nioro 1891 or the 1903 date)

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
